chunks: From him, from Muhammad ibn Abi Hamzah, from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the difference between Ibn Abi Layla and Ibn Shubrumah regarding the black land (fertile land conquered by Muslims) and its owners. I said: Indeed, Ibn Abi Layla said that when they (the non-Muslim owners) embrace Islam, they become free, and the land in their possession belongs to them. As for Ibn Shubrumah, he claimed that they are slaves (or remain in a state of servitude regarding the land) and that the land in their possession does not belong to them. He (peace be upon him) said: 'Regarding the land, it is as Ibn Shubrumah said.' And he said: 'Regarding the men, it is as Ibn Abi Layla said, that when they embrace Islam, they become free.' And with this, there is a statement that I did not memorize.

key_terms.أَحْرَارٌ: Free men (as opposed to slaves or serfs)
key_terms.ابْنُ أَبِي لَيْلَى: A prominent early jurist known for his opinions on land tax and status
key_terms.ابْنُ شُبْرُمَةَ: A jurist whose opinion differed from Ibn Abi Layla regarding land ownership
key_terms.السَّوَاد: Fertile land (specifically in Iraq), often referring to conquered lands
key_terms.عَبِيدٌ: Slaves or those in a state of servitude

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on the ownership of conquered land and the status of its non-Muslim owners in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith resolves the classical juristic debate regarding the conquest of fertile lands (al-Sawad) by affirming a dual ruling: the land remains in the possession of its owners (aligning with Ibn Shubrumah) while the owners retain their personal freedom upon conversion (aligning with Ibn Abi Layla). This synthesis highlights the Shia scholarly approach to reconciling differing Sunni legal opinions, emphasizing that conquest does not automatically entail enslavement or immediate state confiscation of private property. It underscores the principle that Islamic governance respects existing property rights and personal liberty even during territorial expansion.
